lessons.title: Qi Is Not "Energy"
lessons.blurb_en: The single biggest translation mistake in Chinese medicine — and why it matters.
lessons.blurb_zh: 中醫裡最常見的一個翻譯錯誤，也是最該先弄懂的一件事。
paras: When people first encounter Chinese medicine, they almost always meet the word qi in translation as "energy." This translation feels natural, but it causes more confusion than it solves. Energy, in the scientific sense, is something you can measure, store, and convert from one form into another. Qi is not that kind of thing. It is not a substance sitting somewhere, waiting to be used — it is closer to the body doing its work. When someone's qi is described as weak, the point is not that a battery has run low. The point is that the body's basic functions are not being carried out with full force.

This is one reason many teachers of Chinese medicine now leave the word qi untranslated, the same way English speakers keep words like karma and nirvana rather than force them into an English equivalent. Once qi becomes "energy," the next question is almost always the same: can this be measured with a machine? That question has already gone wrong, because it assumes qi is a quantity in the first place. Asking how much qi someone has is a bit like asking how much fitness a person has. Fitness is real — you can see its effects in how someone moves, breathes, and recovers from illness — but it is not a substance sitting inside the body, waiting to be weighed.

So the very first lesson in Chinese medicine has nothing to do with herbs or acupuncture. It is simply this: qi describes a pattern of function, not a form of energy. Get this distinction right, and every idea that follows — from the five functions of qi to the causes of fatigue — will rest on solid ground.
paras_zh: 第一次接觸中醫的人，幾乎都會先遇到「氣」被翻譯成 energy。這個翻譯聽起來很自然，卻製造了比它解決的還多的誤解。科學意義上的 energy 是可以被測量、儲存、轉換形式的東西；氣不是那種東西。氣不是放在某處等著被使用的物質，而更接近「身體正在運作」這件事本身。說某人氣虛，意思不是電池沒電了，而是身體的基本功能沒有被全力執行。

這是為什麼許多中醫老師現在傾向保留 qi 這個字不翻譯——就像英文使用者保留 karma、nirvana 這些字，而不硬找一個英文對應詞。一旦氣被譯成 energy，下一個問題幾乎必然出現：這可以用儀器測量嗎？這個問題從一開始就走錯了方向，因為它預設了氣是一種數量。問一個人有多少氣，有點像問一個人有多少 fitness。fitness 是真實的——你可以從一個人的動作、呼吸、病後恢復力看出它的效果——但它不是身體裡等著被秤重的一種物質。
所以中醫的第一課，跟藥草或針灸都沒有關係。它只是這件事：氣描述的是一種功能的模式，不是一種能量的形式。把這個分野弄對，後面所有的道理——從氣的五個功能，到疲勞的成因——才站得住腳。
questions: According to the passage, what is the difference between "energy" in the scientific sense and qi?
Why do many teachers of Chinese medicine prefer to leave the word qi untranslated?
What does the comparison between qi and "fitness" help explain?
answers: Energy can be measured, stored, and converted between forms, while qi describes the body's functions being carried out — it isn't a substance that exists on its own.
Because translating qi as "energy" invites the wrong kind of question, such as whether it can be measured with a machine, when qi was never meant to describe a measurable quantity.
It shows that something can be real and observable in its effects without being a physical substance that can be stored or weighed.

lessons.title: The Five Jobs of Qi
lessons.blurb_en: Why weak qi makes a person tired, cold, and prone to catching colds — traced back to one principle, not a list to memorize.
lessons.blurb_zh: 氣虛的人為什麼會累、會冷、常常感冒？從一個原理往下推，不用背清單。
paras: Chinese medicine describes qi as doing five jobs in the body. It moves things along — pushing blood through the vessels, fluids through their channels, and the organs through their daily work. It keeps the body warm, which is why healthy hands and feet stay comfortably warm rather than cold. It defends the body against outside threats, which is why some people catch a cold at the first change of season while others seem to shrug it off. It holds things in their place, keeping blood inside the vessels and sweat from leaking out for no reason. And it transforms what a person eats and drinks into something the body can actually use.

These five jobs are not five separate topics to memorize. They are five expressions of the same underlying activity. Once you understand them as one thing seen from five angles, the symptoms of weak qi stop looking like a random list and start looking like a single pattern, read backward. If qi cannot move things along, a person feels tired and doesn't want to talk. If it cannot keep the body warm, the hands and feet turn cold. If it cannot defend the body, colds become frequent. If it cannot hold things in place, a person may sweat without any exertion at all. If it cannot transform food into something usable, appetite drops even though the person is eating normally.

This is the real difference between understanding a principle and memorizing a checklist. A checklist of five symptoms is easy to forget. A principle that explains why those five symptoms show up together — and predicts a sixth one you haven't seen yet — is much harder to lose.
paras_zh: 中醫講氣在身體裡做五件事：推動——把血液推過血管、把水液推過通道、把臟腑推動去做每天的工作；溫煦——維持體溫，這是為什麼健康的手腳是舒服地溫暖，而不是冰冷；防禦——抵擋外來的威脅，這是為什麼有人一換季就感冒，有人卻好像完全不受影響；固攝——把東西固定在該在的位置，讓血液留在血管裡、汗不會無緣無故流出來；還有氣化——把吃進去、喝進去的東西轉變成身體真正能用的東西。
這五件事不是五個要分別背下來的主題，而是同一個底層活動從五個角度看出來的樣子。一旦你把它們理解成一件事，氣虛的症狀就不再像是一份隨機的清單，而是同一個模式倒過來讀。推不動，人就會累、不想講話；溫不了，手腳就會冰冷；防不住，就常常感冒；固不住，可能無緣無故就流汗；化不了，就算正常吃飯，食慾也會下降。
這正是「理解一個原理」跟「背一份檢查清單」的真正差別。五個症狀的清單很容易忘記；一個能解釋這五個症狀為什麼會一起出現——還能預測你還沒看過的第六個症狀——的原理，卻很難丟掉。
questions: List the five jobs of qi described in the passage.
Why does the passage say these five jobs are "not five separate topics to memorize"?
According to the passage, what happens to a person's appetite when qi cannot transform food properly, and why?
answers: Moving things along, keeping the body warm, defending against outside threats, holding things in place, and transforming food and drink into something usable.
Because they are five expressions of one underlying activity — once qi is weak, all five show up as one connected pattern, not five random, unrelated problems.
Appetite drops, even though the person may be eating a normal amount, because the body isn't turning food into something it can actually use.

lessons.title: When Overexertion Drains Qi
lessons.blurb_en: Four ancient characters explain the most common cause of weak qi — and "overexertion" means more than physical tiredness.
lessons.blurb_zh: 《黃帝內經》四個字講完氣虛最常見的成因，而「勞」不只是體力上的累。
paras: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, one of the oldest texts in Chinese medicine, states the idea in four characters: overexertion drains qi. The same chapter goes even further, claiming that a hundred diseases arise from qi. What makes this idea useful today is what counts as "overexertion." It is not limited to physical labor. Thinking too much, carrying responsibility for too long, and never quite letting go of a worry are all treated as forms of overexertion in Chinese medicine — the same category as working a double shift.

Qi behaves like any resource that gets spent. If it is drawn on constantly and never replenished, the result is depletion. And the classic signs of depleted qi line up closely with the five functions from the last lesson: a person feels tired and doesn't want to talk, catches colds easily, and may sweat with the smallest amount of exertion.
None of this is a diagnosis. It is a description of a mechanism — spending without replenishing — that anyone can recognize in their own life, long before it becomes a medical problem.
paras_zh: 《黃帝內經》——中醫最古老的典籍之一——用四個字講完了這個概念：勞則氣耗。同一篇甚至講得更重：百病生於氣。這個概念到今天還有用的地方，在於什麼算是「勞」。它不只限於體力勞動。思慮過度、長期承擔責任、放不下一個擔心，在中醫裡都被當成「勞」的一種——跟連上兩班一樣算在同一個範疇裡。
氣的行為就像任何會被花掉的資源。如果持續被支出、卻從來沒有回補，結果就是耗竭。而氣耗竭的典型徵象，剛好對上上一課的五個功能：人會累、不想講話、容易感冒，稍微用一點力就可能流汗。
這些都不是診斷，而是一種機制的描述——支出而不回補——任何人都能在自己的生活裡認出來，早在它變成醫療問題之前。
questions: What does the phrase "overexertion drains qi" mean, according to the passage?
According to the passage, why does worrying for a long time count as a kind of "overexertion," even without physical labor?
How do the symptoms described in this passage connect to the five functions of qi from the previous lesson?
answers: It means that qi is used up when a person is overexerted — whether the exertion is physical, mental, or emotional.
Because Chinese medicine treats sustained worry and responsibility as a drain on the same resource — qi — that physical labor draws on.

The symptoms — tiredness, frequent colds, and sweating with little exertion — are what happens when qi's five functions (moving, warming, defending, holding, transforming) are no longer being carried out with full force.

lessons.title: Restoring Qi Without Medicine
lessons.blurb_en: The basic principle for restoring qi has nothing to do with herbs — the hard part is following through.
lessons.blurb_zh: 補氣的大原則其實很簡單，而且不需要吃藥——難的是做到。
paras: If overexertion drains qi, then restoring it should, in theory, be simple: spend less, and replenish more. Chinese medicine turns this into four practical habits. Reduce the mental load of constant worry and responsibility. Go to sleep earlier, ideally before eleven at night, when the body's yang qi is naturally being nourished. Eat and drink with some restraint, rather than relying on cold or raw food. And avoid sweating to excess, since heavy sweating draws directly on qi.

These four habits are not four unrelated tips picked at random. Each one addresses a different one of the five functions from earlier in this course. Reducing mental load cuts down on what qi has to move. Sleeping earlier increases how much qi gets replenished overnight. Eating with restraint keeps the transforming function from being overworked. Avoiding excessive sweating protects the holding function from being forced to work overtime.

In other words, the four habits are the same five-function framework, simply read in reverse: instead of asking what happens when qi runs low, they ask what protects it from running low in the first place. None of them require a prescription. All of them require follow-through, which is precisely why they are harder than they sound.
paras_zh: 如果勞則氣耗，理論上要補氣就該很簡單：少支出，多回補。中醫把它變成四個具體的生活習慣：減少思慮與責任帶來的心理負荷；早點睡，理想上在晚上十一點以前，這時身體的陽氣正在被滋養；飲食有所節制，不要靠冰的或生冷的食物；避免過度流汗，因為大量流汗會直接耗損氣。
這四個習慣不是四個隨機挑出來、彼此無關的小撇步。每一個都對應著這門課前面提過的五功能裡的不同一項。減少心理負荷，減少了氣需要去推動的量；早睡，增加了夜間氣被回補的量；飲食節制，避免了氣化功能被過度使用；避免過度流汗，保護了固攝功能不被迫超時工作。
換句話說，這四個習慣就是同一套五功能框架，只是反過來讀：不是問氣不足時會發生什麼，而是問要怎麼保護氣，不讓它一開始就不足。這些都不需要藥方；需要的是持之以恆——這正是為什麼它們聽起來簡單，做起來卻困難。
questions: List the four habits for restoring qi described in the passage.
How does the passage connect these four habits to the five functions of qi taught earlier in the course?
According to the last paragraph, why are these habits harder than they sound?
answers: Reducing mental load, sleeping earlier, eating and drinking with restraint, and avoiding excessive sweating.

Each habit protects a specific function — reducing mental load lightens what qi must move, earlier sleep increases replenishment, restrained eating protects the transforming function, and avoiding excess sweat protects the holding function.
Because none of them require a prescription — they only require consistent follow-through, which is harder to sustain than following a one-time instruction.

lessons.title: Explaining Qi to a Friend
lessons.blurb_en: A model explanation for when a friend asks, "What is qi?" — built from everything covered in this unit.
lessons.blurb_zh: 當朋友問「氣是什麼？」，一段可以直接照講的示範回答，整合這個單元學過的一切。
paras: Suppose a friend who has never studied Chinese medicine asks, "What is qi?" A good answer follows a specific order, because getting the order right is what keeps the conversation from going in the wrong direction. Start here: "Qi isn't a substance you store — it's closer to the body doing its work. When we say someone's qi is weak, we're not saying a battery ran low; we're saying the body's functions aren't being carried out with full force."

Next, explain what those functions are: "In Chinese medicine, qi does five things: it moves things along, keeps you warm, defends you, holds things in place, and turns what you eat into something your body can use." Only after this should the conversation turn to measurement, because that question will come up regardless: "It's not a measurable quantity in the physics sense — it's a way of describing patterns of function. Asking how much qi there is is a bit like asking how much fitness someone has: real, observable in its effects, but not a substance sitting somewhere."

Finally, close with the boundary that matters most: "None of this replaces seeing a doctor. Qi is a framework for understanding how the body works as a whole — not a diagnosis, and not a substitute for one." Explaining qi well is not about finding a clever English word to replace it. It's about walking someone through the idea in an order that keeps them from getting stuck on the wrong question too early.
paras_zh: 假設一位從沒學過中醫的朋友問：「氣是什麼？」一個好的回答要按照特定的順序來講，因為順序對了，對話才不會走偏。可以這樣開始：「氣不是一種你儲存起來的物質，它更接近身體正在運作這件事本身。當我們說一個人氣虛，不是在說電池沒電了，而是在說身體的功能沒有被全力執行。」
接著，解釋這些功能是什麼：「在中醫裡，氣做五件事：它推動事物、讓你保持溫暖、保護你、把東西固定住、把你吃的東西變成身體能用的東西。」只有講完這些之後，才輪到談測量，因為這個問題遲早會被問到：「從物理學的意義上，它不是一個可以測量的量——它是一種描述功能模式的方式。問氣有多少，有點像問一個人有多少 fitness：真實存在、能從它的效果看出來，但不是放在某處等著被秤重的一種物質。」
最後，用最重要的那條邊界收尾：「這一切都不能取代看醫生。氣是理解身體如何整體運作的一個框架——不是診斷，也不能替代診斷。」把氣解釋好，重點不是找到一個聰明的英文字來取代它，而是用一個順序帶著對方走過這個概念，不讓他們太早卡在錯的問題上。

It shows that something can be real and observable in its effects without being a physical substance that can be measured or stored, which helps the listener let go of the "energy" framework.
Because without that boundary, a listener might mistakenly think the explanation is offering medical advice, rather than a cultural and theoretical framework.

lessons.title: Yin and Yang Are Not "Good" and "Bad"
lessons.blurb_en: The most common misreading of yin-yang, corrected before it can cause any more confusion.
lessons.blurb_zh: 陰陽最常見的誤解，先在這裡糾正過來。
paras: After qi, the next idea a student of Chinese medicine meets is yin and yang — and the most common misunderstanding arrives almost immediately. In popular culture, yin often gets treated as "bad" or "dark" and yang as "good" or "light," the way a villain and a hero get cast in a story. Chinese medicine uses the words very differently. Yin and yang describe a pair of complementary functions, not a moral judgment. Yin is associated with substance, rest, cooling, and the body's interior; yang is associated with function, activity, warming, and the body's exterior. Neither one is better than the other, in the same way that inhaling is not "better" than exhaling.

The two also cannot exist without each other. A body with no yin — no substance, no fluids, no rest — would have nothing for yang to warm or move. A body with no yang — no function, no activity, no warmth — would have substance sitting perfectly still, doing nothing. Health, in this framework, is not about maximizing yang and minimizing yin, or the reverse. It is about the two staying in a working relationship with each other, each doing its job without overtaking the other.

This is why a Chinese medicine practitioner almost never says a patient has "too much yin" or "too little yang" as a final verdict. Those words only mean something in relation to each other, at a particular moment, for a particular person. Learning yin-yang is really learning to stop asking "which one is winning" and start asking "are they still working together."
paras_zh: 學完氣之後，中醫學生接下來會遇到的下一個概念是陰陽——而最常見的誤解幾乎馬上就會出現。在流行文化裡，陰常被當成「壞的」或「黑暗的」，陽被當成「好的」或「光明的」，就像故事裡的反派跟英雄。中醫用這兩個字的方式完全不同。陰陽描述的是一對互補的功能，不是道德判斷。陰跟物質、休息、寒涼、身體的內部有關；陽跟功能、活動、溫熱、身體的外部有關。兩者沒有誰比較好，就像吸氣不會比呼氣「更好」一樣。
這兩者也無法脫離對方單獨存在。一個完全沒有陰——沒有物質、沒有津液、沒有休息——的身體，會讓陽無物可溫、無物可推動。一個完全沒有陽——沒有功能、沒有活動、沒有溫熱——的身體，物質會完全靜止，什麼都做不了。在這個框架裡，健康不是把陽最大化、把陰最小化，或反過來。健康是讓兩者維持一種持續運作的關係，各自做好自己的工作，不壓過對方。
這就是為什麼中醫師幾乎不會把「陰太多」或「陽太少」當成一個最終定論來講。這些字只有在彼此相對、在特定時刻、對特定的人身上才有意義。學陰陽，其實是在學怎麼停止問「哪一個贏了」，開始問「他們還有沒有一起運作」。

lessons.title: How Qi Deficiency Splits Into Yang and Yin
lessons.title_zh: 氣虛怎麼分成陽虛與陰虛
lessons.blurb_en: Qi deficiency has a direction — and knowing which one changes what actually helps.
lessons.blurb_zh: 氣虛是有方向的——弄清楚哪個方向，才知道什麼真的有幫助。
paras: The first unit of this course ended with qi deficiency — a state where the body's basic functions are not being carried out with full force. Once yin and yang enter the picture, qi deficiency can be described more precisely, because it can lean in one of two directions. When the "warming" and "moving" side of qi runs low, the result is called yang deficiency: a person feels cold, especially in the hands and feet, moves slowly, and often prefers warm drinks and warm weather. When the "cooling" and "moistening" side runs low instead, the result is called yin deficiency: a person may feel warm in the afternoon or evening, have a dry mouth, and sleep restlessly despite feeling tired.

It helps to picture qi as a single team that yin and yang split between them. Yang qi handles warming and moving; yin qi handles moistening and calming. Plain qi deficiency is a general shortage of staff. Yang deficiency and yin deficiency describe which side of the team is short-staffed. A person can, in theory, have signs of both at once, which is simply qi deficiency that has not yet settled clearly into one direction.

None of this is something to self-diagnose from a reading passage. What matters here is the logic: Chinese medicine rarely stops at a single, flat label like "weak qi." It keeps asking a more specific question — weak in which direction — because the answer changes what actually helps.
paras_zh: 這門課的第一個單元最後停在氣虛——身體的基本功能沒有被全力執行的狀態。陰陽這個概念加進來之後，氣虛可以講得更精確，因為它可以偏向兩個方向的其中一個。當氣裡「溫煦」和「推動」的那一側不足，結果叫做陽虛：人會怕冷，尤其是手腳，動作變慢，通常偏好溫熱的飲料和天氣。當「滋潤」和「安定」的那一側不足，結果叫做陰虛：人可能在下午或傍晚覺得燥熱，口乾，雖然疲倦卻睡不安穩。
把氣想像成一支被陰陽兩邊分掉的隊伍會比較好理解。陽氣負責溫煦和推動；陰氣負責滋潤和安定。單純的氣虛是整體人手不足；陽虛跟陰虛講的是隊伍的哪一邊人手不足。理論上一個人可以同時有兩邊的跡象，那只是還沒明確偏向某一個方向的氣虛。
這些都不是要你從一篇閱讀文章裡自我診斷。這裡重要的是背後的邏輯：中醫很少停在一個籠統的標籤，像是「氣虛」，就結束。它會繼續問一個更具體的問題——虛在哪個方向——因為答案會改變真正有幫助的做法。
questions: According to the passage, what is the difference between yang deficiency and yin deficiency?
Why does the passage compare qi to "a single team that yin and yang split between them"?
According to the last paragraph, why does Chinese medicine avoid stopping at a flat label like "weak qi"?
answers: Yang deficiency is a shortage of the warming/moving side of qi (cold, slow, prefers warmth), while yin deficiency is a shortage of the cooling/moistening side (afternoon warmth, dry mouth, restless sleep despite tiredness).

Because it helps explain that yang qi and yin qi handle different jobs within the same overall resource — general qi deficiency is a shortage of the whole team, while yang or yin deficiency describes which side is short-staffed.
Because asking "weak in which direction" gives a more specific answer, and that more specific answer is what actually changes what kind of help is appropriate.

lessons.title: The Four Relationships Between Yin and Yang
lessons.blurb_en: Opposition, interdependence, waxing-waning, and transformation — four angles on the same moving system.
lessons.blurb_zh: 對立制約、互根互用、消長平衡、相互轉化——同一個系統的四個角度。
paras: Chinese medicine describes yin and yang as connected through four different kinds of relationship, and each one answers a different question about how change happens in the body. The first is opposition: yin and yang restrain each other, the way cold restrains heat and heat restrains cold. If one grows unchecked, it naturally holds the other back. The second is interdependence: neither one can exist without the other, the way a shadow cannot exist without light. Yin provides the substance that yang acts on; yang provides the activity that keeps yin from becoming stagnant.

The third relationship is called waxing and waning: yin and yang do not stay fixed — they shift back and forth constantly, the way day gradually gives way to night and back again. A small increase in one is normally matched by a small decrease in the other, keeping the overall balance steady. The fourth relationship is transformation: under the right conditions, yin can convert into yang and yang can convert into yin, the way water can become steam and steam can become water again. This is the relationship that explains sudden change — a long illness marked by cold, quiet symptoms (yin) can, at a certain point, suddenly flip into a hot, agitated state (yang), and Chinese medicine treats this as a known pattern, not a mystery.

These four relationships are not four separate rules to memorize in isolation. They describe one continuously moving system, seen from four different angles: how the two hold each other in check, how they depend on each other, how they shift gradually, and how they can suddenly flip. Together, they explain why "balance" in Chinese medicine is never a fixed point — it is a moving target that a healthy body keeps hitting, over and over, without ever settling into one extreme.
paras_zh: 中醫講陰陽之間有四種不同的關係，每一種都回答身體裡「變化怎麼發生」的一個不同問題。第一種是對立制約：陰陽互相牽制，就像冷會抑制熱、熱也會抑制冷。如果其中一個不受限制地增長，另一個自然會把它拉回來。第二種是互根互用：兩者都無法脫離對方獨立存在，就像影子不能沒有光而存在。陰提供物質讓陽去作用；陽提供活動讓陰不至於停滯。

第三種關係叫做消長平衡：陰陽不是固定不變的——它們持續來回移動，就像白天逐漸讓位給黑夜，再逐漸回到白天。一方小幅增加，通常會對應另一方小幅減少，讓整體維持穩定。第四種關係是相互轉化：在適當的條件下，陰可以轉變成陽，陽也可以轉變成陰，就像水可以變成蒸氣，蒸氣也可以再變回水。這個關係解釋了突然的變化——一場以寒冷、安靜症狀（陰）為主的長期疾病，可能在某個時間點突然翻轉成燥熱、躁動的狀態（陽），中醫把這當成一個已知的模式，不是一個謎。
這四種關係不是四條要分開背誦的規則。它們描述的是同一個持續在動的系統，從四個不同的角度看：兩者怎麼互相牽制、怎麼互相依存、怎麼漸進地移動、又怎麼會突然翻轉。合起來，它們解釋了為什麼中醫講的「平衡」從來不是一個固定的點——它是一個健康的身體不斷重新命中的移動目標，不會停在某一個極端上。
questions: According to the passage, what is the difference between the "opposition" relationship and the "interdependence" relationship between yin and yang?
What everyday comparison does the passage use to explain the "waxing and waning" relationship?
According to the passage, how does the "transformation" relationship explain a sudden change in illness, such as a cold state suddenly becoming a hot one?
answers: Opposition means yin and yang restrain each other so neither grows unchecked, like cold and heat holding each other back, while interdependence means neither can exist without the other, like light and shadow.
The passage compares it to day gradually giving way to night and back again, with small shifts in one side matched by small shifts in the other.

It explains that under the right conditions, yin can convert into yang (and the reverse), the way water can become steam — so a long, cold, quiet illness can suddenly flip into a hot, agitated state, following a known pattern rather than being a mystery.

lessons.title: Reading Your Own Yin-Yang Balance
lessons.blurb_en: Four everyday signs — temperature, energy, thirst, sleep — and why only the pattern over time matters.
lessons.blurb_zh: 體溫、精神、口渴、睡眠——四個日常觀察，重點是長期的模式，不是單一一天。
paras: Chinese medicine offers a simple, everyday way to notice which direction a person's yin and yang currently lean, long before anything becomes a medical problem. The signs are ordinary: temperature preference, energy through the day, thirst, and sleep. A person leaning toward yang excess or yin deficiency tends to run warm, prefer cold drinks, feel most energetic in the afternoon or evening, and sleep lightly or restlessly. A person leaning toward yang deficiency tends to run cold, especially in the hands and feet, prefer warm drinks, feel most sluggish in the morning, and sleep heavily but wake up unrefreshed.

None of these signs mean anything on their own. A single cold morning does not make someone "yang deficient," any more than one sleepless night makes someone "yin deficient." What matters is a pattern that holds steady over weeks, not an isolated day. This is also why Chinese medicine asks so many small, seemingly unrelated questions in a consultation — thirst, sleep, sweating, appetite, mood — because no single answer is diagnostic by itself. The pattern across all of them is.

The purpose of noticing these patterns in daily life is not to self-treat. It is to know your own baseline well enough to notice when something changes, and to describe that change clearly to a doctor. "I've been sleeping restlessly and craving cold drinks for the last month" is a far more useful sentence to bring into a clinic than "I don't feel like myself."
paras_zh: 中醫提供了一個簡單、日常就能觀察的方法，讓人能注意到自己的陰陽目前偏向哪個方向——遠在任何事情變成醫療問題之前。這些跡象都很平常：體溫偏好、一天中的精神狀態、口渴程度、睡眠品質。偏向陽亢或陰虛的人，通常容易覺得燥熱、偏好冰涼的飲料、在下午或傍晚精神最好、睡得淺或不安穩。偏向陽虛的人，通常容易怕冷，尤其是手腳，偏好溫熱的飲料，早上精神最差，睡得沉但醒來不解乏。
這些跡象單獨看都沒有意義。一個寒冷的早晨不能讓一個人變成「陽虛」，就像一個失眠的夜晚不能讓一個人變成「陰虛」。重要的是一個持續好幾週、穩定出現的模式，而不是單一一天的狀態。這也是為什麼中醫問診時會問許多看似不相關的小問題——口渴、睡眠、流汗、食慾、情緒——因為沒有任何單一答案本身能拿來診斷。所有答案合起來的模式才是關鍵。
在日常生活裡注意這些模式，目的不是自己治療。目的是清楚了解自己的基準狀態，好在有變化時能注意到，並且能把那個變化清楚地描述給醫師聽。「我這一個月睡得不安穩，很想喝冰的」比「我覺得不太對勁」對看診有用得多。
questions: According to the passage, what four everyday signs does Chinese medicine use to notice a person's yin-yang tendency?
Why does the passage say a single cold morning does not make someone "yang deficient"?
According to the last paragraph, what is the real purpose of noticing these patterns in daily life?
answers: Temperature preference, energy through the day, thirst, and sleep quality.
Because what matters is a pattern that holds steady over weeks, not a single, isolated day — one instance doesn't establish a lasting tendency.
Not to self-treat, but to know your own baseline well enough to notice a real change and describe it clearly to a doctor.

lessons.title: Excess Heat and Deficient Heat Are Not the Same Thing
lessons.blurb_en: Two patients both feel hot — but one has too much yang, and the other has too little yin. Same symptom, opposite cause.
lessons.blurb_zh: 兩個人都覺得燥熱——一個是陽太多，一個是陰太少。同一個症狀，相反的成因。
paras: A patient who feels hot doesn't automatically have "too much heat" in the way English speakers imagine a fever. Chinese medicine distinguishes two very different mechanisms behind a feeling of heat, and confusing them leads to exactly the wrong approach. The first is excess heat: yang itself has grown too strong, the way a fire burns hotter than it should. This kind of heat tends to be intense, constant, and accompanied by a strong thirst for cold drinks, a red face, and a loud, forceful voice.

The second is deficient heat, and it works by subtraction rather than addition: yin — the cooling, moistening, restraining substance — has become too thin to hold yang in check, so yang appears to run hot simply because nothing is containing it anymore. This kind of heat tends to be milder, shows up specifically in the afternoon or evening, and comes with a dry mouth that doesn't demand much water, flushed cheekbones, and night sweats rather than daytime sweating.

The distinction matters because the response runs in opposite directions. Excess heat calls for clearing and draining — cooling the fire down directly. Deficient heat calls for nourishing yin — refilling what's missing so yang has something to be held by again. Treating deficient heat as if it were excess heat, by cooling aggressively without replenishing yin, is a common and unhelpful mismatch — which is exactly why this distinction is left to a trained diagnosis, not a symptom checklist.
paras_zh: 一個覺得燥熱的病人，不代表身體裡「熱太多」，就像英文使用者想像發燒那樣。中醫把「熱」這種感覺背後區分成兩種非常不同的機制，把它們搞混會導向完全錯誤的方向。第一種是實熱：陽本身變得太強，就像一團燒得比該有的還旺的火。這種熱通常強烈、持續，伴隨著想喝冰水的強烈口渴、滿臉通紅，還有洪亮、有力的聲音。
第二種是虛熱，它的運作方式是「減法」而不是「加法」：陰——那個負責寒涼、滋潤、牽制的物質——變得太薄弱，沒辦法再把陽扣住，於是陽看起來很燥熱，只是因為已經沒有東西在約束它了。這種熱通常比較輕微，特別會在下午或傍晚出現，伴隨著不太想喝很多水的口乾、顴骨發紅，還有夜間盜汗，而不是白天流汗。
這個區分很重要，因為對應的做法方向完全相反。實熱需要清熱瀉火——直接把那團火降下來。虛熱需要滋陰——把缺少的東西補回來，讓陽重新有東西可以被扣住。把虛熱當成實熱來處理，用力清熱卻不滋陰，是一個常見又沒有幫助的誤配——這正是為什麼這個區分要交給受過訓練的診斷，而不是一份症狀清單。
questions: According to the passage, what mechanism causes "excess heat," and what symptoms are associated with it?
According to the passage, what mechanism causes "deficient heat," and what symptoms are associated with it?
According to the last paragraph, why does the passage say treating deficient heat as if it were excess heat is "a common and unhelpful mismatch"?
answers: Excess heat is caused by yang itself growing too strong, like a fire burning hotter than it should; it's associated with intense, constant heat, strong thirst for cold drinks, a red face, and a loud voice.

Deficient heat is caused by yin becoming too thin to hold yang in check; it's associated with milder heat specifically in the afternoon or evening, a dry mouth without much thirst, flushed cheekbones, and night sweats.

Because the correct responses run in opposite directions — excess heat calls for cooling and draining, while deficient heat calls for nourishing yin — so cooling aggressively without replenishing yin fails to address the actual mechanism.

quiz.q: According to the passage, what is the cause of "excess heat"?
options: Yin becoming too thin to hold yang in check.
Yang itself growing too strong.
A complete absence of both yin and yang.
Cold weather exposure.

quiz.q: According to the passage, which symptom is specifically associated with deficient heat rather than excess heat?
options: A loud, forceful voice.
Night sweats and flushed cheekbones in the afternoon or evening.
Strong thirst for cold drinks.
A constantly red face all day.

quiz.q: According to the last paragraph, why do excess heat and deficient heat need opposite responses?
options: Because they are actually the exact same condition.
Because one is caused by too much yang and the other by too little yin, so cooling directly helps one but not the other.
Because deficient heat doesn't actually exist.
Because excess heat is always more dangerous than deficient heat.

lessons.boundary_en: This lesson explains a diagnostic distinction, not a way to self-treat. Telling excess heat from deficient heat requires a licensed practitioner's examination, not just a feeling of warmth.
lessons.boundary_zh: 這是診斷區分的說明，不是自我治療的方法；分辨實熱與虛熱需要合格醫師的診察，不能只靠燥熱的感覺自行判斷。

lessons.title: The Temperature of Food Has Nothing to Do With a Thermometer
lessons.blurb_en: Why ginger is "warming" and watermelon is "cooling" even when both are served at room temperature.
lessons.blurb_zh: 為什麼薑是「溫」的、西瓜是「涼」的，即使兩者都是常溫端上桌。
paras: Chinese medicine assigns every food a temperature nature — cold, cool, neutral, warm, or hot — and the label has nothing to do with the food's actual physical temperature. A bowl of watermelon straight out of a hot summer garden is still classified as "cold" in nature, and a cup of ginger tea served lukewarm is still "warm." The nature describes the effect the food tends to produce in the body after it's eaten, not the temperature on a thermometer.

Cooling foods, like watermelon, cucumber, and mung beans, are traditionally used to clear heat and generate fluids, which is why they're especially popular in the summer heat this course discussed in the seasonal unit. Warming foods, like ginger, cinnamon, and lamb, are traditionally used to dispel cold and support yang, which is why they show up so often in winter cooking. Neutral foods, like rice and most staple grains, sit in the middle and rarely push a person's balance in either direction.

The practical use of this system isn't to sort foods into "good" and "bad" categories — that would just recreate the mistake this course corrected in an earlier unit about yin and yang. The use is matching a food's tendency to a person's current state: a person already running warm gains less from more warming foods, and a person already running cold gains little from a diet of only cooling ones. Food temperature, read this way, is simply another application of the same yin-yang logic covered throughout this course.
paras_zh: 中醫給每一種食物都分配了一種寒熱性質——寒、涼、平、溫、熱——而這個標籤跟食物實際的物理溫度毫無關係。一碗剛從炎熱夏日花園裡端出來的西瓜，性質上仍然被分類成「寒」；一杯溫溫的薑茶，仍然是「溫」的。這個性質描述的是這個食物吃下去之後，傾向在身體裡產生什麼效果，不是溫度計量出來的溫度。
涼性的食物，像西瓜、小黃瓜、綠豆，傳統上被用來清熱生津，這也是為什麼它們在這門課節氣單元討論過的夏天特別受歡迎。溫性的食物，像薑、肉桂、羊肉，傳統上被用來驅寒助陽，這也是為什麼它們在冬天的料理裡這麼常出現。平性的食物，像米飯和大部分主食穀類，位在中間，很少把一個人的平衡明顯推向任何一個方向。
這套系統實際的用途，不是把食物分成「好」跟「壞」的類別——那只會重演這門課稍早在陰陽單元裡糾正過的那個錯誤。它的用途，是把食物的傾向對應到一個人目前的狀態：一個本來就偏燥熱的人，吃更多溫性食物得到的好處有限；一個本來就偏怕冷的人，只吃涼性食物也得不到什麼好處。用這個角度來看，食物的寒熱性質，只是這門課從頭到尾都在講的同一套陰陽邏輯的另一個應用。
questions: According to the passage, what does a food's "temperature nature" actually describe?
According to the passage, why are cooling foods like watermelon especially popular in summer?
According to the last paragraph, what is the "practical use" of the food temperature system, and what mistake does it avoid repeating?
answers: The effect the food tends to produce in the body after it's eaten, not its actual physical temperature.
Because cooling foods are traditionally used to clear heat and generate fluids, matching the season's need discussed in the seasonal wellness unit.

Matching a food's tendency to a person's current state, rather than sorting foods into "good" and "bad" categories — avoiding the same mistake corrected earlier about treating yin and yang as good versus bad.

quiz.q: According to the passage, what does a food's temperature nature in Chinese medicine actually describe?
options: The temperature shown on a thermometer.
The effect the food tends to produce in the body after it's eaten.
How long the food takes to cook.
The country the food originally came from.

quiz.q: According to the passage, why are ginger, cinnamon, and lamb classified as "warming" foods?
options: Because they are always served hot.
Because they are traditionally used to dispel cold and support yang.
Because they contain no nutrients.
Because they are only eaten in summer.

quiz.q: According to the last paragraph, what mistake does the food temperature system avoid repeating?
options: Treating yin and yang, or "cooling" and "warming," as simply good versus bad.
Assigning any temperature nature to food at all.
Matching food to the season.
Discussing food in a health context.

lessons.boundary_en: This lesson explains a general framework for food properties, not dietary treatment. Specific dietary changes for a health condition should be discussed with a licensed doctor.
lessons.boundary_zh: 這是食物性質的一般框架說明，不是飲食治療；針對特定健康狀況的飲食調整，應該與合格醫師討論。

lessons.title: When Yin and Yang Split Apart
lessons.blurb_en: The most serious four characters in this entire course — and why they describe an ending, not just an imbalance.
lessons.blurb_zh: 這整門課裡最沉重的四個字——以及它們為什麼描述的是一個終點，不只是失衡。
paras: Every lesson in this unit has treated yin and yang as two things that shift, argue, and rebalance — sometimes yang runs a little high, sometimes yin runs a little low, and the whole system is built around correcting that drift. The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic describes a much more serious possibility with a phrase that translates roughly as "when yin and yang split apart, the vital essence is exhausted." This isn't describing an imbalance to be corrected. It's describing the complete failure of the relationship itself — the point at which yin and yang stop interacting entirely.

This phrase is traditionally read as describing death, or the process immediately leading to it, which is why it carries more weight than any of the everyday imbalances discussed elsewhere in this course. Every other lesson has assumed yin and yang are still, in some form, talking to each other — restraining, depending on, and converting into each other. "Splitting apart" describes the one condition where that conversation has ended for good.

The reason this idea belongs in an introductory course, rather than being left out as too dark a topic, is that it clarifies everything that came before it. If health is yin and yang staying in a working relationship, and death is that relationship ending completely, then every lesson on restoring balance in this course has actually been about the same underlying goal, just applied to smaller, correctable versions of the same basic problem: keeping the conversation between yin and yang going.
paras_zh: 這個單元裡的每一課，都把陰陽當成兩個會移動、會拉扯、會重新找到平衡的東西——有時候陽稍微偏高，有時候陰稍微偏低，整套系統都是圍繞著修正這種偏移建構起來的。《黃帝內經》用一句大概可以翻譯成「陰陽離決，精氣乃絕」的話，描述了一個嚴重得多的可能性。這不是在描述一個該被修正的失衡。它描述的是這段關係本身徹底的失敗——陰陽完全停止互動的那個時刻。
這句話傳統上被讀成在描述死亡，或緊接在死亡之前的過程，這也是為什麼它比這門課別處討論過的任何日常失衡都要沉重。這門課別的每一課，都假設陰陽以某種形式仍然在互相對話——互相牽制、互相依存、互相轉化。「離決」描述的是那個對話徹底結束的唯一狀態。
這個概念之所以屬於一門入門課程，而不是因為太沉重被留在外面，是因為它把之前的一切都講清楚了。如果健康是陰陽維持一種持續運作的關係，而死亡是那段關係徹底結束，那麼這門課裡每一課關於恢復平衡的內容，其實都在談同一個底層的目標，只是應用在同一個基本問題的更小、還能被修正的版本上：讓陰陽之間的對話繼續下去。
questions: According to the passage, how has every other lesson in this unit treated yin and yang, compared to what "splitting apart" describes?
According to the passage, what is "splitting apart" traditionally read as describing?
According to the last paragraph, why does this idea belong in an introductory course rather than being left out?
answers: Every other lesson has treated yin and yang as things that shift, argue, and rebalance, still interacting in some form; "splitting apart" describes the complete failure of that relationship, where the interaction stops entirely.
Death, or the process immediately leading to it.

Because it clarifies everything that came before — health is yin and yang staying in a working relationship, and every lesson on restoring balance has really been about the same underlying goal of keeping that relationship going, just applied to smaller, correctable problems.

quiz.q: According to the passage, what have all the other lessons in this unit assumed about yin and yang?
options: That they never interact at all.
That they are still, in some form, interacting with each other.
That they are identical to each other.
That only yang exists in a healthy body.

quiz.q: According to the passage, what does the phrase describing yin and yang "splitting apart" traditionally refer to?
options: A minor, easily corrected imbalance.
Death, or the process immediately leading to it.
A normal daily fluctuation.
A seasonal transition.

quiz.q: According to the last paragraph, what underlying goal does the passage say every lesson on restoring balance shares?
options: Achieving a fixed, permanent state that never changes.
Keeping the relationship — the "conversation" — between yin and yang going.
Maximizing yang while eliminating yin completely.
Avoiding all mention of illness or death.

lessons.boundary_en: This lesson explains a classical concept, not a way to assess anyone's condition. Any concern about a serious or worsening health state should go to a doctor immediately, not to this reading.
lessons.boundary_zh: 這是經典概念的說明，不是拿來評估任何人狀況的工具；對嚴重或惡化的健康狀態有疑慮，應該立刻就醫，而不是參考這篇文章。

lessons.blurb_en: A model answer for "Isn't yin-yang just a martial-arts symbol?" — built from everything covered in this unit.
lessons.blurb_zh: 當朋友問「陰陽不就是武術符號嗎？」，一段整合這個單元學過內容的示範回答。
paras: Suppose a friend asks, "Isn't yin-yang just a symbol from martial arts movies?" A good answer starts by separating the symbol from the idea. The black-and-white circle is a visual summary, not the concept itself, and the concept is worth explaining on its own terms: "Yin and yang describe two complementary functions in the body — substance and activity, cooling and warming, rest and movement. Neither one is 'good' or 'bad.' They're more like inhaling and exhaling: both necessary, neither one superior."

Next, it helps to explain why the idea matters practically, not just philosophically: "When a doctor of Chinese medicine says someone's yang is weak, they mean the warming and moving side of the body's functions isn't strong enough — the person feels cold, moves slowly, prefers warmth. It's a description of function, the same way saying someone has 'low energy' describes a pattern without claiming to have found a single broken part." This keeps the explanation grounded in something concrete rather than mystical.

Finally, it's worth naming what yin-yang is not: "It's not a fixed personality type, and it's not a horoscope. It's not something a person 'is' once and for all — it shifts throughout the day, the seasons, and a person's life, and a doctor's job is to notice which direction it's currently leaning, not to hand out a permanent label." Ending on this note keeps a friend from walking away thinking yin-yang works like a zodiac sign.
paras_zh: 假設一位朋友問：「陰陽不就是武術電影裡的一個符號嗎？」一個好的回答要先把符號跟概念分開。黑白相間的圓形圖案是一種視覺上的濃縮，不是概念本身，概念值得用它自己的方式來解釋：「陰陽描述的是身體裡兩種互補的功能——物質與活動、寒涼與溫熱、休息與活動。沒有哪一個是『好』或『壞』的。它們比較像吸氣跟呼氣：兩者都是必要的，沒有誰比較優越。」
接著，解釋這個概念為什麼在實際上有意義，而不只是哲學上有意義會有幫助：「當中醫師說一個人的陽虛，意思是身體功能裡溫煦與推動的那一側不夠強——這個人會怕冷、動作變慢、偏好溫暖。這是一種功能上的描述，就像說一個人『沒什麼精神』是在描述一種模式，而不是聲稱找到了某個壞掉的零件。」這讓解釋保持在具體的層面，而不是神祕的層面。
最後，值得講清楚陰陽不是什麼：「它不是一種固定的人格類型，也不是星座。它不是一個人一次性、永久地『就是』什麼——它會隨著一天、季節、一個人的人生階段而改變，醫師的工作是注意它目前偏向哪個方向，而不是發一個永久的標籤。」用這句話收尾，能避免朋友離開時覺得陰陽的運作方式就像星座一樣。

lessons.title: The Five Elements Are Categories, Not Chemicals
lessons.blurb_en: Wood, fire, earth, metal, water — five patterns of behavior, not five physical ingredients.
lessons.blurb_zh: 木火土金水——五種行為模式，不是五種物質成分。
paras: The phrase "Five Elements" — wood, fire, earth, metal, and water — sounds, to an English speaker, like an ancient and mistaken attempt at chemistry, the way early Greek thinkers once proposed that everything was made of four elements. Chinese medicine is not making a claim about chemistry at all. The five elements are a classification system, a way of sorting phenomena — organs, seasons, emotions, colors, tastes, even sounds — into five families based on shared patterns of behavior, not shared physical substance.

Wood describes things associated with growth, flexibility, and upward movement — spring, the color green, the emotion of anger, a shoot pushing through soil. Fire describes things associated with heat, activity, and rising — summer, the color red, joy, a flame reaching upward. Earth describes things associated with stability, nourishment, and centering — late summer, the color yellow, worry, soil that holds and feeds a plant's roots. Metal describes things associated with contraction, clarity, and letting go — autumn, the color white, grief, a blade that cuts cleanly. Water describes things associated with stillness, storage, and downward movement — winter, the color black, fear, water pooling at the lowest point.

None of these five categories describes a physical ingredient inside the body. They describe a pattern — the same way saying someone has a "fiery temper" doesn't mean flames are involved. Once the five elements are read as five patterns rather than five materials, the rest of the system stops sounding mystical and starts sounding like what it actually is: an organizing chart for how different parts of a person, and different parts of nature, tend to behave.
paras_zh: 「五行」——木、火、土、金、水——這個說法對英語使用者來說，聽起來像是一種古老又錯誤的化學嘗試，就像古希臘思想家曾經主張萬物由四種元素組成一樣。中醫在這裡完全不是在講化學。五行是一套分類系統，一種把現象——臟腑、季節、情緒、顏色、味道，甚至聲音——依照共同的行為模式（不是共同的物質）分成五個家族的方法。

木描述的是跟生長、柔韌、向上移動有關的事物——春天、綠色、憤怒這個情緒、一根從土裡冒出來的嫩芽。火描述的是跟熱、活動、向上升有關的事物——夏天、紅色、喜悅、一團向上竄的火焰。土描述的是跟穩定、滋養、居中有關的事物——長夏、黃色、憂慮、能承接並滋養植物根部的土壤。金描述的是跟收斂、清晰、放下有關的事物——秋天、白色、悲傷、一把切割乾淨俐落的刀刃。水描述的是跟靜止、儲藏、向下移動有關的事物——冬天、黑色、恐懼、匯聚到最低點的水。
這五個類別沒有一個是在描述身體裡的某種物質成分。它們描述的是一種模式——就像說一個人「脾氣火爆」不代表真的有火焰參與其中。一旦把五行讀成五種模式而不是五種物質，這套系統的其餘部分就不再聽起來神祕，而會開始聽起來像它實際的樣子：一張整理「一個人的不同部分、以及自然界的不同部分，傾向怎麼表現」的組織圖。

lessons.title: The Generating Cycle
lessons.blurb_en: Wood feeds fire, fire feeds earth — a mother-child chain that explains why weakness can travel.
lessons.blurb_zh: 木生火、火生土——一條母子鏈，解釋虛弱為什麼會轉移到別的地方。
paras: Once the five elements are understood as five patterns rather than five materials, the next question is how they relate to each other — and Chinese medicine describes two main cycles. The first is the generating cycle, often described as a parent-child or mother-child relationship: each element feeds and supports the next one in a fixed sequence. Wood generates fire, the way dry wood feeds a flame. Fire generates earth, the way a fire's ash becomes soil. Earth generates metal, the way ore is formed and mined from the ground. Metal generates water, the way condensation forms on a cold metal surface. And water generates wood, the way water nourishes a growing tree, completing the circle back to where it started.

This cycle matters in Chinese medicine because organs are mapped onto the five elements, and the generating relationship describes how organs support one another under normal, healthy conditions. The kidney (water) is said to nourish the liver (wood); the liver nourishes the heart (fire); the heart nourishes the spleen (earth); the spleen nourishes the lung (metal); and the lung nourishes the kidney again, closing the loop. When one organ in this chain is running low, the "child" organ downstream may eventually run low too, simply from not being fed enough.

The generating cycle is not a claim that one organ literally manufactures another. It is a way of describing dependency: weakness in one place can show up, with a delay, somewhere else entirely — and a doctor familiar with this cycle knows to look upstream, at the "parent," rather than only treating the symptom where it finally appeared.
paras_zh: 一旦五行被理解成五種模式而不是五種物質，下一個問題就是它們彼此之間的關係——中醫描述了兩個主要的循環。第一個是相生的循環，常被形容成一種母子關係：每個元素依照固定的順序滋養、支持下一個元素。木生火，就像乾木餵養火焰一樣。火生土，就像火燒過的灰燼變成土壤一樣。土生金，就像礦石從地底被形成、開採出來一樣。金生水，就像冰冷的金屬表面會凝結出水珠一樣。水生木，就像水滋養一棵成長中的樹一樣，讓循環回到起點，完整地繞了一圈。
這個循環在中醫裡很重要，因為臟腑被對應到五行，而相生的關係描述的是臟腑在正常、健康的狀態下如何互相支持。腎（水）滋養肝（木）；肝滋養心（火）；心滋養脾（土）；脾滋養肺（金）；肺再滋養腎，把循環閉合起來。當這條鏈裡的某個臟腑不足時，下游的「子」臟腑最終也可能因為得不到足夠的滋養而跟著不足。
相生的循環並不是在主張某個臟腑真的在製造另一個臟腑。它是一種描述依存關係的方式：某個地方的虛弱，可能延遲一段時間後，在完全不同的地方顯現出來——熟悉這個循環的醫師，知道要往上游、往「母」臟腑去看，而不是只治療症狀最後出現的那個地方。

answers: Wood generates fire (like dry wood feeding a flame), fire generates earth (like ash becoming soil), earth generates metal (like ore forming in the ground), metal generates water (like condensation on cold metal), and water generates wood (like water nourishing a tree).

The kidney (water) nourishes the liver (wood), the liver nourishes the heart (fire), the heart nourishes the spleen (earth), the spleen nourishes the lung (metal), and the lung nourishes the kidney again.

It describes a dependency relationship, not literal manufacturing — weakness in one organ can show up later in a "downstream" organ, so a doctor familiar with the cycle looks upstream at the "parent" organ rather than only treating where the symptom appears.

lessons.title: The Controlling Cycle
lessons.blurb_en: Wood controls earth, earth controls water — the safety mechanism that keeps each element in check.
lessons.blurb_zh: 木克土、土克水——讓每個元素不至於過度擴張的安全機制。
paras: Alongside the generating cycle, Chinese medicine describes a second relationship among the five elements: the controlling cycle, which keeps any one element from growing unchecked. Wood controls earth, the way tree roots break through and hold soil in place. Earth controls water, the way a riverbank contains a flood. Water controls fire, the way water extinguishes flame. Fire controls metal, the way heat melts and shapes metal. And metal controls wood, the way an axe cuts down a tree, closing this cycle as well.

Mapped onto the organs, this cycle explains why a problem in one place can create a problem somewhere else that looks, at first, unrelated. The liver (wood) is said to control the spleen (earth). When a person experiences prolonged frustration or anger — associated with the liver — that strain can, over time, show up as digestive trouble, the domain of the spleen. A patient describing "stress that upsets my stomach" is, in this framework, describing exactly this relationship, even without using its vocabulary.

The controlling cycle is a safety mechanism, not a punishment. Under normal conditions, each element checks the next one just enough to keep it from overreaching — the way a good editor checks a writer's excesses without silencing them. Illness, in this view, often isn't a single part malfunctioning in isolation. It's a checking relationship that has become too strong, too weak, or badly timed.
paras_zh: 除了相生循環之外，中醫還描述了五行之間的第二種關係：相剋循環，用來阻止任何一個元素不受限制地增長。木克土，就像樹根穿透並固定住土壤一樣。土克水，就像河岸圍住洪水一樣。水克火，就像水澆熄火焰一樣。火克金，就像高溫熔化並塑形金屬一樣。金克木，就像斧頭砍倒一棵樹一樣，也讓這個循環閉合起來。
把這個循環對應到臟腑上，可以解釋為什麼一個地方的問題，一開始看起來會在另一個看似不相關的地方造成問題。肝（木）被認為會克脾（土）。當一個人長期經歷挫折或憤怒——跟肝有關——那股壓力久而久之，可能會以消化方面的問題表現出來，那是脾的領域。一位病人描述「壓力大到胃都不舒服」，在這個框架下，即使沒用到這套詞彙，講的正是這種關係。
相剋循環是一種安全機制，不是一種懲罰。在正常情況下，每個元素只會恰到好處地牽制住下一個，讓它不至於過度擴張——就像一位好編輯會節制作者的過度之處，而不是讓作者噤聲。在這個觀點下，生病往往不是單一部分孤立地故障，而是一種牽制關係變得太強、太弱，或時機不對。

lessons.title: Matching Organs to Elements
lessons.blurb_en: Why liver, gallbladder, and anger belong to the same category — and how that explains symptom clusters.
lessons.blurb_zh: 為什麼肝、膽、憤怒屬於同一個類別——這如何解釋一群看似不相關的症狀。
paras: Chinese medicine assigns each of the five elements to a pair of organs, and this mapping is what makes the five-element system practically useful rather than purely decorative. Wood is matched to the liver and gallbladder. Fire is matched to the heart and small intestine. Earth is matched to the spleen and stomach. Metal is matched to the lung and large intestine. Water is matched to the kidney and bladder. Each pairing also comes with an associated emotion, season, and sense organ — anger with the liver, joy with the heart, worry with the spleen, grief with the lung, and fear with the kidney.

This matching is not anatomical in the Western sense — the "liver" in this system is a wider functional category than the organ a surgeon would remove, and it includes functions modern anatomy assigns elsewhere. What the mapping is genuinely useful for is noticing clusters of symptoms that, on the surface, look unrelated. A person under prolonged frustration who also develops a bitter taste in the mouth, tension headaches, and irregular digestion is, in this framework, showing a cluster that traces back to one element — wood — rather than four separate, coincidental problems.

This is the real payoff of learning the five elements: not memorizing five categories for their own sake, but gaining a way to notice when several seemingly unrelated complaints are actually one pattern wearing different disguises. Chinese medicine calls this "treating the root rather than the branch" — and the five-element map is one of the main tools for finding the root in the first place.
paras_zh: 中醫把五行的每一個都對應到一對臟腑，而這個對應正是讓五行系統真正實用、而不只是裝飾性的關鍵。木對應肝與膽。火對應心與小腸。土對應脾與胃。金對應肺與大腸。水對應腎與膀胱。每一對搭配也都伴隨著一種情緒、一個季節、一個感覺器官——肝配憤怒，心配喜悅，脾配憂慮，肺配悲傷，腎配恐懼。
這種對應不是西方意義上的解剖學對應——這套系統裡的「肝」是一個比外科醫師會摘除的那個器官更廣的功能類別，它包含了現代解剖學分配到別處的一些功能。這個對應真正有用的地方，是能注意到表面上看似不相關的一群症狀。一個長期處在挫折中、同時嘴巴發苦、有緊張性頭痛、消化又不規律的人，在這個框架下，展現的是一群可以追溯回同一個元素——木——的症狀群，而不是四個各自獨立、剛好同時發生的問題。
這才是學五行真正的收穫：不是為了背誦五個類別本身，而是獲得一種能力，能注意到好幾個看似不相關的抱怨，其實是同一個模式換了不同的偽裝出現。中醫把這叫做「治本不治標」——而五行對照表正是找到「本」的主要工具之一。

Because the "liver" in this system is a wider functional category that includes functions modern anatomy assigns elsewhere, not a strict anatomical match.
Not memorizing five categories for their own sake, but gaining the ability to notice when several seemingly unrelated complaints are actually one pattern showing up in different forms.

lessons.title: When the Controlled Element Rebels
lessons.blurb_en: Metal is supposed to control wood — but what happens when wood grows strong enough to attack back?
lessons.blurb_zh: 金本來應該克木——但如果木長得夠強大，反過來攻擊回去呢？
paras: The controlling cycle from earlier in this unit describes a stable arrangement: each element keeps the next one in check, the way metal controls wood by cutting it down. But Chinese medicine also describes what happens when that arrangement breaks — a pattern called "rebellion," in which the element that's supposed to be controlled grows so strong that it overwhelms its controller instead, reversing the direction of the relationship entirely.

A concrete version of this shows up in the liver-lung relationship. Metal (the lung) normally controls wood (the liver), the way a blade keeps a tree in check. But if the liver becomes excessively strong — from prolonged frustration, for instance — it can overwhelm the lung instead, a pattern sometimes described as "wood insulting metal." A person in this pattern may show liver-type symptoms, like irritability, alongside lung-type symptoms, like coughing or shortness of breath, in a combination that looks backward compared to the expected controlling direction.

Naming this pattern matters because it stops a doctor from assuming the five-element relationships are a fixed, one-way script. The generating and controlling cycles describe the normal, healthy traffic pattern; rebellion describes what it looks like when one element has grown powerful enough to run the traffic pattern in reverse. Recognizing rebellion is part of recognizing that the five-element system describes tendencies under normal conditions, not unbreakable laws.
paras_zh: 這個單元稍早的相剋循環，描述的是一種穩定的安排：每個元素都牽制著下一個，就像金克木、用刀刃砍伐樹木一樣。但中醫也描述了這個安排崩解時會發生什麼事——一種叫做「反侮」的模式，本來該被控制的元素變得太強大，反過來壓制了控制它的那一方，把這段關係的方向整個反過來。
一個具體的版本出現在肝肺關係上。金（肺）本來控制木（肝），就像刀刃牽制著樹木一樣。但如果肝變得過度強盛——舉例來說，因為長期的挫折感——它可能反過來壓制肺，這種模式有時被稱為「木侮金」。處在這種模式裡的人，可能同時出現肝型的症狀，像易怒，以及肺型的症狀，像咳嗽或呼吸急促，這種組合看起來跟預期中的相剋方向正好相反。
為這個模式命名很重要，因為它讓醫師不會假設五行的關係是一套固定、單向的劇本。相生跟相剋循環描述的是正常、健康狀態下的運行模式；反侮描述的是當一個元素變得強大到能反過來操控整個運行模式時，會是什麼樣子。認識反侮，是認識到五行系統描述的是正常條件下的傾向，而不是不可打破的定律的一部分。

answers: The normal controlling cycle describes a stable arrangement where each element keeps the next in check; "rebellion" describes what happens when the controlled element grows so strong it overwhelms its controller instead, reversing the direction.

It describes the liver (wood) becoming excessively strong — often from prolonged frustration — and overwhelming the lung (metal) instead of being controlled by it, producing both liver-type and lung-type symptoms together.
Because it stops a doctor from assuming the five-element relationships are a fixed, one-way script — recognizing that the system describes tendencies under normal conditions, not unbreakable laws.

lessons.title: Reading a Face by Its Element
lessons.blurb_en: Why a doctor of Chinese medicine looks at your face before you say a word — and what each color and feature is thought to reveal.
lessons.blurb_zh: 為什麼中醫師在你開口之前就先看你的臉——以及每種顏色和部位被認為透露了什麼。
paras: A doctor of Chinese medicine traditionally begins an examination with observation, before a single question is asked, and the five-element framework gives that observation a specific vocabulary. Each element is matched not only to an organ, but to a facial color and a sense organ, treating the face as a kind of visible display panel for what's happening deeper inside the body.

Wood is matched to a greenish or bluish tinge and to the eyes; a person under prolonged liver strain is traditionally said to show it around the eyes first. Fire is matched to redness and the tongue, tying the heart to speech and to a flushed complexion. Earth is matched to a yellowish tinge and the mouth, connecting digestive strength to the color around the lips. Metal is matched to paleness and the nose, and water is matched to a darker, sometimes bluish-black tinge and the ears.

None of this works as a single glance diagnosis — a person's natural skin tone, lighting, and momentary flush from heat or exercise all complicate a reading taken in isolation. The framework's real use is the same as everywhere else in this course: not a single clue treated as conclusive, but one thread in a larger pattern, cross-checked against everything else a trained practitioner asks and observes.
paras_zh: 中醫師傳統上會在問一句話之前，先從觀察開始問診，而五行框架給了這個觀察一套具體的詞彙。每個元素不只對應到一個臟腑，還對應到一種臉部顏色與一個感覺器官，把臉當成身體深處狀況的一種可見顯示面板。
木對應到偏青或偏藍的色調，還有眼睛；一個長期處在肝的壓力下的人，傳統上被認為會先在眼睛周圍顯現出來。火對應到發紅與舌頭，把心跟言語、還有紅潤的氣色連在一起。土對應到偏黃的色調與嘴巴，把消化力的強弱跟嘴唇周圍的顏色連結起來。金對應到蒼白與鼻子，水對應到偏暗、有時偏藍黑的色調與耳朵。
這一切都不能靠看一眼就下診斷——一個人天生的膚色、光線，還有因為熱或運動而暫時發紅，都會讓單獨拿出來看的一個線索變得複雜。這套框架真正的用途，跟這門課別處一樣：不是把單一線索當成定論，而是更大一個模式裡的一條線索，要跟受過訓練的醫師問到、觀察到的其他一切互相對照。

Redness is matched to the Fire element, along with the tongue.

Because a person's natural skin tone, lighting, and momentary flush from heat or exercise all complicate a reading taken in isolation — a single clue needs to be cross-checked against everything else observed, not treated as conclusive on its own.

lessons.title: The Five Flavors, and Why Too Much of a Good Thing Backfires
lessons.blurb_en: Sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty — each flavor is matched to an organ it feeds, and to an organ it can harm in excess.
lessons.blurb_zh: 酸苦甘辛鹹——每種味道都對應著一個它滋養的臟腑，以及一個它過量時可能傷害的臟腑。
paras: Chinese medicine matches five basic flavors to the five elements, following the same logic used for organs, emotions, and colors earlier in this unit: sour to wood and the liver, bitter to fire and the heart, sweet to earth and the spleen, pungent to metal and the lung, and salty to water and the kidney. In small, ordinary amounts, each flavor is traditionally said to support its matched organ — a little sourness aids the liver, a little saltiness supports the kidney.

The twist is that the same flavor, taken to excess, is said to injure the very organ it normally supports, following the same "too much of a good thing" logic covered elsewhere in this course. Excessive salty food is traditionally linked to strain on the kidney and, by extension, on blood vessels — a claim modern nutrition also recognizes in its own vocabulary, linking high sodium intake to blood pressure. Excessive sweet food is linked to strain on the spleen's transforming function, echoing modern concerns about sugar and metabolism.

This isn't a coincidence worth dismissing, nor proof that one system copied the other. It's a case of two very different frameworks, working centuries apart with different tools, arriving at a similar practical conclusion: flavor, taken moderately, supports the body; the same flavor, taken in excess, can work against the very function it once supported.
paras_zh: 中醫把五種基本味道對應到五行，遵循著這個單元稍早用在臟腑、情緒、顏色上的同一套邏輯：酸對應木與肝，苦對應火與心，甘對應土與脾，辛對應金與肺，鹹對應水與腎。在少量、一般的份量下，每種味道傳統上被認為能支持它對應的臟腑——一點點酸味有助於肝，一點點鹹味支持腎。
有趣的轉折是，同一種味道吃過量，被認為會傷害它平常支持的那個臟腑，遵循著這門課別處也提過的同一套「過猶不及」的邏輯。過鹹的食物傳統上被連結到腎、進而連結到血管的負擔——這個主張，現代營養學也用它自己的詞彙認可，把高鈉攝取連結到血壓。過甜的食物被連結到脾的轉化功能的負擔，呼應著現代對糖分與代謝的關注。
這不是一個值得被輕視的巧合，也不是一套系統抄了另一套的證據。這是兩套非常不同的框架，隔了好幾個世紀、用不同的工具，各自抵達了一個相似的實際結論：適量的味道，支持身體；同一種味道吃過量，卻能反過來對抗它原本支持的那個功能。

lessons.title: Explaining the Five Elements to a Friend
lessons.blurb_en: A model answer for "Why does Chinese medicine talk about wood and fire like they're organs?"
lessons.blurb_zh: 當朋友問「為什麼中醫講木跟火，講得好像它們是臟器？」，一段整合這個單元的示範回答。
paras: Suppose a friend asks, "Why does Chinese medicine talk about wood and fire like they're organs?" A good answer starts by naming what the five elements are not: "They're not a claim that your liver is made of wood, and they're not an ancient chemistry theory. They're a classification system — a way of sorting things like organs, emotions, and seasons into five families based on how they behave, not what they're physically made of."

From there, it helps to give one concrete example rather than listing all five: "Take 'wood.' It's associated with growth and upward movement, so it's matched with the liver, the emotion of anger, and springtime — not because they share a material, but because they share a pattern of pushing forward and expanding. When a doctor says stress is 'affecting your wood element,' they mean it's showing up in that whole family of related functions, not that there's actual wood somewhere in your body." This keeps the abstraction tied to something the friend can picture.

Finally, it's worth explaining why doctors bother with the system at all: "The real use is noticing patterns across seemingly unrelated symptoms — irritability, headaches, and digestive trouble showing up together, for example, all pointing back to one element rather than being three separate coincidences. It's a diagnostic tool, not a belief system, and it still ends the same way every lesson in this course does: for anything real, see an actual doctor."
paras_zh: 假設一位朋友問：「為什麼中醫講木跟火，講得好像它們是臟器一樣？」一個好的回答，要先說清楚五行不是什麼：「這不是在說你的肝是木頭做的，也不是一套古老的化學理論。它是一套分類系統——一種把臟腑、情緒、季節這類東西，依照它們怎麼表現（而不是它們物理上是什麼材質）分成五個家族的方法。」
接下來，給一個具體的例子會比列出全部五個更有幫助：「拿『木』來說。它跟生長、向上移動有關，所以被對應到肝、憤怒這個情緒，還有春天——不是因為它們共享同一種材質，而是因為它們共享一種向前推進、向外擴張的模式。當醫師說壓力『在影響你的木』，意思是它正表現在那整個相關功能的家族裡，不是說你身體裡真的有木頭。」這讓抽象的概念保持在朋友能想像得出來的層面。
最後，值得解釋為什麼醫師要費心用這套系統：「真正的用處在於能注意到看似不相關的症狀之間的模式——比方說，易怒、頭痛、消化不良同時出現，全都指回同一個元素，而不是三個各自獨立的巧合。這是一種診斷工具，不是一套信仰系統，而且它的結尾跟這門課每一課一樣：任何真實的健康問題，還是要去看真正的醫師。」

lessons.title: The Organs Are Functions, Not Anatomy
lessons.blurb_en: The single biggest translation trap in Chinese medicine — and it starts with the word "spleen."
lessons.blurb_zh: 中醫裡最大的翻譯陷阱，從「脾」這個字開始。
paras: The biggest translation trap in this entire course arrives with a single word: "spleen." In English, the spleen is a fist-sized organ mostly known for filtering blood and supporting the immune system — most people could not name a single symptom of a damaged one. In Chinese medicine, the spleen (脾) is one of the busiest organs in the entire body: it governs digestion, transforms food into usable qi and blood, and keeps blood contained within the vessels. When a Chinese medicine textbook talks about the "spleen," it is describing a functional system that overlaps only partly with what a Western doctor calls by the same English word.

This is not an isolated mistake limited to one organ. Every organ name in Chinese medicine — liver, heart, lung, kidney — refers to a broader functional category, not a strict anatomical structure. The "kidney" in this system, for example, includes reproductive function and the storage of a person's inherited constitutional strength, roles that Western anatomy assigns to entirely different systems. None of this means Chinese medicine is wrong about anatomy; it means the two systems are answering different questions. Western anatomy asks, "What does this physical structure do?" Chinese medicine asks, "What set of functions travels together, and what should we call that set?"

Once this is understood, a strange-sounding sentence like "the spleen governs digestion" stops sounding like bad biology and starts sounding like what it actually is: a claim within its own coherent system, using a borrowed English word that happens to overlap only partially with its meaning. The organs in this unit should be read as functional categories first, anatomical structures a distant second.
paras_zh: 這整門課裡最大的翻譯陷阱，來自一個字：「脾」。在英文裡，spleen 指的是一個拳頭大小的器官，主要功能是過濾血液、支持免疫系統——多數人連受損的脾臟會有什麼症狀都說不出來。在中醫裡，脾是全身最忙碌的臟腑之一：它主導消化、把食物轉化成能用的氣與血，還負責把血液固攝在血管裡。當中醫教科書講到「脾」，它描述的是一個功能系統，跟西醫用同一個英文字（spleen）指稱的器官，只有部分重疊。

這不是侷限在單一臟腑的個別錯誤。中醫裡的每一個臟腑名稱——肝、心、肺、腎——指的都是一個較廣的功能類別，而不是嚴格的解剖結構。舉例來說，這套系統裡的「腎」，包含了生殖功能，也包含儲存一個人先天體質根本的功能，這些角色在西方解剖學裡被分配到完全不同的系統。這不代表中醫在解剖學上是錯的；意思是這兩套系統在回答不同的問題。西方解剖學問的是：「這個物理結構做什麼？」中醫問的是：「哪一組功能總是一起出現，我們該把這組功能叫做什麼？」
理解這一點之後，「脾主導消化」這種聽起來很怪的句子，就不再像是錯誤的生物學，而會開始聽起來像它實際的樣子：在它自己這套自成一體的系統裡的一個主張，只是借用了一個剛好只有部分重疊的英文字。這個單元裡的臟腑，應該先被讀成功能類別，其次才是解剖結構。

lessons.title: The Five Zang Organs
lessons.blurb_en: Liver, heart, spleen, lung, kidney — five functional systems, read as five case studies of the five elements.
lessons.blurb_zh: 肝心脾肺腎——五個功能系統，是五行框架的五個延伸案例。
paras: The five zang organs — liver, heart, spleen, lung, and kidney — are the five functional systems introduced briefly in the last unit's discussion of the five elements, now explained on their own terms. The liver (wood) is in charge of keeping qi moving smoothly throughout the body; when it's working well, mood stays even and digestion runs without friction. The heart (fire) is said to govern blood circulation and to "house the mind," meaning it's linked to clarity of thought and quality of sleep, not just the physical pumping of blood.

The spleen (earth) governs digestion and transformation, turning food and drink into usable qi and blood, and also keeps blood contained within its vessels. The lung (metal) governs breathing, but also a wider function called "dispersing and descending" — spreading fluids and qi through the body and pushing them downward, which is why it is closely tied to skin health and the body's outer defenses. The kidney (water) stores a person's inherited constitutional strength, governs reproduction and growth, and also handles water metabolism throughout the body.

These five descriptions are meant to be read together, not memorized in isolation. Each zang organ was assigned to an element in the last unit precisely because its function matches that element's pattern — the liver's smooth, upward-moving qi matches wood's pattern of growth; the kidney's storage function matches water's pattern of stillness and depth. Learning the five zang organs is really learning five expanded case studies of the five-element framework already introduced.
paras_zh: 五臟——肝、心、脾、肺、腎——是上一個單元討論五行時簡短提過的五個功能系統，現在用它們自己的方式來解釋。肝（木）負責讓氣在全身順暢地運行；當它運作良好時，情緒會保持平穩，消化也不會有阻滯。心（火）被認為主導血液循環，也「藏神」，意思是它跟思緒的清晰度、睡眠品質有關，不只是物理上推動血液流動。
脾（土）主導消化與轉化，把飲食轉變成能用的氣與血，也負責把血液固攝在血管裡。肺（金）主導呼吸，但也有一個更廣的功能叫做「宣發肅降」——把津液和氣散布到全身，並把它們往下推動，這也是為什麼肺跟皮膚健康、身體的外部防禦密切相關。腎（水）儲存一個人先天的體質根本，主導生殖與生長，也處理全身的水液代謝。
這五個描述應該合在一起讀，而不是分開背誦。上一個單元裡，每個臟腑之所以被對應到一個元素，正是因為它的功能符合那個元素的模式——肝那種順暢、向上運行的氣，符合木生長的模式；腎的儲藏功能，符合水靜止、深沉的模式。學五臟，其實就是在學已經介紹過的五行框架的五個延伸案例。

lessons.title: The Six Fu Organs
lessons.blurb_en: Stomach, intestines, gallbladder, bladder, and the mysterious "triple burner" — organs built for movement, not storage.
lessons.blurb_zh: 胃、腸、膽、膀胱，還有神祕的「三焦」——為了流通而生的臟腑，不是為了儲存。
paras: Alongside the five zang organs, Chinese medicine describes six fu organs: the gallbladder, small intestine, stomach, large intestine, bladder, and a sixth called the "triple burner," which has no single equivalent in Western anatomy. The zang organs are traditionally described as solid and as storing vital substances — qi, blood, and fluids. The fu organs are traditionally described as hollow, and their job is to receive, transform, and pass things along, rather than to store them long-term.

The stomach receives food and begins breaking it down, passing it to the small intestine, which further separates what the body will absorb from what it will discard. The large intestine receives that waste and governs its final transformation and elimination. The gallbladder stores and releases bile to aid digestion, and the bladder stores and releases urine. The triple burner is the odd one out: rather than a single organ, it describes three functional zones — upper, middle, and lower — that together manage the movement of fluids and qi through the entire torso.

The pattern across all six is "movement and passage" rather than "storage." A useful way to remember the difference: the zang organs are like a warehouse, holding onto valuable resources; the fu organs are like a series of loading docks, built for things to keep moving through them. Neither type of organ is more important than the other — a warehouse with no loading docks has nothing coming in or going out, and loading docks with no warehouse have nothing worth moving.
paras_zh: 除了五臟之外，中醫還描述了六腑：膽、小腸、胃、大腸、膀胱，還有第六個叫做「三焦」，在西方解剖學裡沒有單一的對應。五臟傳統上被描述為實心的，負責儲存重要的物質——氣、血、津液。六腑傳統上被描述為中空的，它們的工作是接收、轉化、傳遞東西，而不是長期儲存。
胃接收食物並開始分解，再傳給小腸，小腸進一步把身體要吸收的部分跟要排掉的部分分開。大腸接收那些廢物，主導最後的轉化與排出。膽儲存並釋放膽汁來幫助消化，膀胱儲存並釋放尿液。三焦是比較特別的一個：它不是單一的臟器，而是描述三個功能區域——上焦、中焦、下焦——合起來管理津液與氣在整個軀幹裡的運行。
這六個共同的模式是「運行與傳遞」，而不是「儲存」。有一個好記的方法：五臟像倉庫，保存著珍貴的資源；六腑像一連串的裝卸碼頭，是為了讓東西持續流通而建的。這兩種臟腑沒有哪一種比較重要——沒有裝卸碼頭的倉庫，什麼都進不來也出不去；沒有倉庫的裝卸碼頭，也沒有值得搬運的東西。

lessons.title: How Zang and Fu Organs Pair Up
lessons.blurb_en: Why heart trouble can show up as a burning sensation elsewhere — the logic behind zang-fu pairing.
lessons.blurb_zh: 為什麼心的問題可能會表現在完全不相關的地方——臟腑配對背後的邏輯。
paras: Each of the five zang organs is paired with one of the six fu organs — the liver with the gallbladder, the heart with the small intestine, the spleen with the stomach, the lung with the large intestine, and the kidney with the bladder (the triple burner is paired separately, with the heart's supporting structure). Chinese medicine calls this an "interior-exterior" relationship: the zang organ is the interior partner, doing the deeper, storing work, while the fu organ is the exterior partner, doing the more exposed, processing work.

The pairing means the two organs' problems often travel together. A common example: heat building up in the heart can travel to its paired organ, the small intestine, and show up as a burning sensation during urination — a symptom that, read on its own, seems to have nothing to do with the heart at all. Another example: a struggling spleen (digestion and transformation) commonly shows up alongside a struggling stomach (initial breakdown of food) — nausea and poor appetite appearing together, rather than as two coincidental complaints.

This pairing logic is one reason a Chinese medicine consultation can feel like it's asking about seemingly unrelated body systems at once. It isn't scattered questioning — it's checking both halves of a known partnership, because a problem rarely stays confined to just one side of it.
paras_zh: 五臟裡的每一個，都跟六腑裡的一個配對——肝配膽、心配小腸、脾配胃、肺配大腸、腎配膀胱（三焦則另外配對，跟心的輔助結構有關）。中醫把這叫做「表裡」關係：臟是裡（內部）的一方，做較深層、儲存性質的工作；腑是表（外部）的一方，做較外顯、處理性質的工作。
這個配對意味著兩個臟腑的問題常常會一起出現。一個常見的例子：心裡積聚的熱，可能傳到它配對的臟腑——小腸，表現成小便灼熱——這個症狀單獨看，似乎跟心完全沒關係。另一個例子：脾（消化與轉化）出問題，常常會伴隨著胃（食物初步分解）也出問題——噁心和食慾不振同時出現，而不是兩個各自獨立、剛好同時發生的抱怨。
這種配對邏輯，是為什麼中醫問診有時候感覺像是同時在問好幾個看似不相關的身體系統。這不是漫無目的地亂問——是在檢查一組已知搭檔的兩個半邊，因為問題很少只侷限在其中一邊。

lessons.title: The Heart as Emperor: Organs as a Government
lessons.blurb_en: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic describes each organ as an official with a government job — and the metaphor is more useful than it sounds.
lessons.blurb_zh: 《黃帝內經》把每個臟腑描述成一個有官職的官員——這個比喻比聽起來更有用。
paras: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic organizes the entire set of organs covered in this unit using a single extended metaphor: a royal court, with each organ holding a specific government post. The heart is named "the ruler," responsible for the overall direction of the whole body, the way an emperor sets the direction of a kingdom without personally performing every task. The lung is named "the prime minister," managing the flow of qi throughout the body the way a minister manages the flow of resources and orders through a government.

The liver is named "the general," in charge of planning and strategy — a fitting role for the organ this course has already connected to smooth, forward-moving qi and to anger when that movement is blocked. The spleen and stomach are named officials in charge of granaries and storage, responsible for the intake and processing that feeds everyone else in the "government." Each title isn't decoration; it's a compressed description of the organ's role relative to all the others.

The real value of the metaphor is what it says about failure. A kingdom doesn't collapse because one official had a single bad day — it collapses when officials stop coordinating, when the ruler's direction isn't being carried out, or when one office starts overreaching into another's duties. Reading illness this way shifts the question from "which single part is broken" to "where has the coordination between offices broken down" — the same systems-level thinking this entire unit has been building toward.
paras_zh: 《黃帝內經》用一個延伸的比喻，把這個單元涵蓋的整組臟腑組織起來：一個朝廷，每個臟腑擔任一個特定的官職。心被稱為「君主之官」，負責整個身體的整體方向，就像皇帝設定一個國家的方向，而不用親自執行每一件事。肺被稱為「相傅之官」，管理全身氣的流動，就像一位宰相管理著政府裡資源與命令的流動。
肝被稱為「將軍之官」，負責規劃與謀略——這個角色，剛好對應著這門課稍早已經連結過的、順暢向前運行的氣，以及那個運行受阻時出現的憤怒。脾與胃被稱為負責倉廩、儲藏的官員，負責攝入與處理，餵養這個「朝廷」裡的每一個人。每一個官銜都不是裝飾；它是這個臟腑相對於所有其他臟腑角色的一種濃縮描述。
這個比喻真正的價值，在於它對「失敗」的講法。一個朝廷不會因為某個官員某一天表現不好就垮台——它會垮台，是因為官員們停止協調、君主的方向沒有被執行下去，或是某個官署開始越權侵犯到另一個官署的職責。用這個角度來讀疾病，把問題從「哪個單一部分壞掉了」，轉移到「哪裡的官署間協調出了問題」——正是這整個單元一直在建構的那種系統層級的思考方式。

lessons.title: The Brain, According to Chinese Medicine
lessons.blurb_en: Neither zang nor fu — where does the brain actually fit in this system, and why does it get its own category?
lessons.blurb_zh: 既不是臟也不是腑——腦在這套系統裡到底放在哪裡，為什麼它需要自己的類別？
paras: A natural question, after two full lessons on the five zang organs and six fu organs, is: where is the brain in all of this? The honest answer is that it doesn't fit cleanly into either category, and Chinese medicine solves the problem by giving it, along with a small group of other structures, a third category entirely: the "extraordinary organs," which includes the brain, bone marrow, bones, blood vessels, the uterus, and — despite being listed among the fu organs earlier — the gallbladder, which is considered to straddle both categories.

The extraordinary organs share a defining feature: like the zang organs, they are solid and store something important, but unlike the zang organs, they aren't matched to one of the five elements or paired with a fu organ. The brain specifically is described as "the sea of marrow," filled and nourished by the kidney's stored constitutional strength — which is why this course's earlier lesson on the kidney's role in growth and reproduction is also, indirectly, a lesson about what's believed to keep the brain properly nourished over a lifetime.

This category exists because Chinese medicine's organ system was never meant to force every structure into one of two boxes. The extraordinary organs are the system's own acknowledgment that some things — the brain very much included — don't behave like either a storing zang organ or a processing fu organ, and needed their own place in the framework rather than being awkwardly squeezed into one that didn't fit.
paras_zh: 讀完兩整課的五臟與六腑之後，一個自然的問題是：腦在這一切裡放在哪裡？誠實的答案是，它沒辦法乾淨地放進任何一個類別，而中醫解決這個問題的方式，是給它、連同一小群其他結構，一個完全獨立的第三類別：「奇恆之腑」，包括腦、骨髓、骨、脈、女子胞（子宮），還有——儘管前面已經被列在六腑裡——被認為橫跨兩個類別的膽。
奇恆之腑共享一個決定性的特徵：像五臟一樣，它們是實心的，儲存著重要的東西，但跟五臟不同，它們沒有被對應到五行的其中一個，也沒有跟一個腑配對。腦特別被描述成「髓海」，由腎儲藏的體質根本填充、滋養——這也是為什麼這門課稍早關於腎在生長與生殖上角色的那一課，同時也間接是一堂關於什麼被認為能讓腦一輩子維持適當滋養的課。
這個類別之所以存在，是因為中醫的臟腑系統從來不打算把每一個結構都硬塞進兩個盒子的其中一個。奇恆之腑是這套系統自己的承認：有些東西——腦絕對包括在內——的表現既不像儲存性質的臟，也不像處理性質的腑，需要在這套框架裡有自己的位置，而不是被彆扭地塞進一個不合身的類別裡。

Because Chinese medicine's organ system was never meant to force every structure into one of two boxes — the extraordinary organs are the system's acknowledgment that some structures don't behave like either a storing zang organ or a processing fu organ.

lessons.title: Qi, Blood, and Body Fluids: The Organs' Raw Materials
lessons.blurb_en: The organs in this unit don't just have functions — they produce and manage three substances that make everything else possible.
lessons.blurb_zh: 這個單元裡的臟腑不只有功能——它們還生產並管理三種讓一切得以運作的物質。
paras: This unit has described what each organ does, but not yet what, specifically, the organs are working with. Chinese medicine names three core substances that the organs produce, circulate, and depend on: qi, already covered in detail in the first unit of this course; blood, which nourishes and moistens the body as it circulates, produced through the combined work of the spleen's transformation and the heart's governing of circulation; and body fluids, a broader category covering everything from saliva and sweat to the fluid that keeps joints moving.

These three aren't independent of each other — they're produced from the same raw materials and constantly convert into and support one another. Qi is said to move blood, the way a pump moves water; blood is said to be the material foundation that qi needs to move through. Body fluids and blood share such a close relationship that heavy blood loss is traditionally expected to affect fluid levels, and severe fluid loss, in turn, is expected to affect blood.

Thinking of qi, blood, and fluids as one interconnected system, rather than three separate topics, explains why a single cause — say, a struggling spleen, discussed earlier in this unit — can ripple outward into fatigue (a qi problem), a pale complexion (a blood problem), and dry skin (a fluid problem) all at once. The organs aren't just doing separate jobs in this unit; they're collaborating on producing and managing this same shared set of three raw materials.
paras_zh: 這個單元描述了每個臟腑做什麼，但還沒描述臟腑實際上在處理的是什麼。中醫指出三種臟腑生產、運行、並依賴的核心物質：氣，這門課第一個單元已經詳細講過；血，在循環的過程中滋養並滋潤身體，由脾的轉化與心對循環的主導共同運作而產生；還有津液，一個較廣的類別，涵蓋從唾液、汗水，到讓關節保持活動的液體等一切。
這三者不是互相獨立的——它們由同樣的原料生產出來，並持續互相轉化、互相支持。氣被認為推動血，就像幫浦推動水一樣；血被認為是氣需要藉以運行的物質基礎。津液跟血的關係緊密到，大量失血傳統上被預期會影響津液的量，而嚴重的津液流失，反過來也被預期會影響血。
把氣、血、津液想成一個彼此相連的系統，而不是三個各自獨立的主題，解釋了為什麼一個原因——比方說，這個單元稍早討論過的脾出問題——能同時擴散成疲倦（氣的問題）、臉色蒼白（血的問題），和皮膚乾燥（津液的問題）。這個單元裡的臟腑不只是各自做著獨立的工作；它們是在共同生產、管理著同一套共享的三種原料。

lessons.title: Explaining Zang-Fu to a Friend
lessons.blurb_en: A model answer for "Wait, isn't the spleen just part of your immune system?"
lessons.blurb_zh: 當朋友問「等等，脾不就是免疫系統的一部分嗎？」，一段整合這個單元的示範回答。
paras: Suppose a friend, hearing that Chinese medicine talks about the spleen governing digestion, asks, "Wait, isn't the spleen just part of your immune system?" This is the single most useful moment to clarify the whole unit: "In Western anatomy, yes — the spleen mainly filters blood and supports immunity. But in Chinese medicine, 'spleen' is the English translation for a much broader functional category that governs digestion and the transformation of food into qi and blood. The two systems are using the same English word for two different things — it's less like a factual disagreement and more like a translation collision."

From there, it helps to explain the logic of the whole organ system in one sentence: "Chinese medicine sorts the body into five deep, storing organs — the zang — and six surface-level, processing organs — the fu — and pairs them up, so a problem in one often shows up in its partner. That's why a Chinese medicine consultation can ask about your sleep, your digestion, and your mood in the same conversation — it's not random, it's checking connected pairs."

Finally, it's worth closing with the same reminder that ends every lesson in this course: "None of this replaces an actual diagnosis. If you want to know what your spleen, kidney, or any organ is really doing, that's a question for a licensed doctor — Chinese medicine or Western medicine, whichever fits the concern." Naming this boundary clearly is what keeps the whole explanation useful rather than mystifying.
paras_zh: 假設一位朋友聽到中醫說脾主導消化，問：「等等，脾不就是免疫系統的一部分嗎？」這正是釐清整個單元最有用的時刻：「在西方解剖學裡，沒錯——脾主要是過濾血液、支持免疫力。但在中醫裡，『脾』這個英文翻譯，指的是一個廣得多的功能類別，主導消化和把食物轉化成氣與血。兩套系統用同一個英文字指稱兩件不同的事——與其說是事實上的分歧，不如說是一場翻譯上的碰撞。」
接下來，用一句話解釋整個臟腑系統的邏輯會有幫助：「中醫把身體分成五個深層、儲存性質的臟——五臟——和六個表層、處理性質的腑——六腑——再把它們配對起來，所以一個地方的問題常常會表現在它的搭檔身上。這就是為什麼中醫問診會在同一次對話裡問你的睡眠、消化、情緒——這不是隨機的，是在檢查有連結的配對。」
最後，值得用這門課每一課都用的同一句提醒來收尾：「這一切都不能取代真正的診斷。如果你想知道你的脾、腎，或任何一個臟腑實際上在做什麼，那是合格醫師才能回答的問題——中醫或西醫都可以，看你關心的是哪一種。」把這條界線講清楚，才能讓整個解釋保持有用，而不是變得神祕難懂。

lessons.title: Meridians Are Maps, Not Pipes
lessons.blurb_en: Why no meridian has ever been found under a microscope — and why that isn't the problem it sounds like.
lessons.blurb_zh: 為什麼從來沒有任何一條經絡在顯微鏡下被找到——以及這為什麼不是聽起來的那種問題。
paras: When Western readers first hear about meridians — the channels along which qi is said to travel — the natural assumption is that they must be physical tubes, something like blood vessels or nerves, just not yet found by modern dissection. This assumption is understandable, but it leads to a dead end. No meridian has ever been isolated under a microscope as a distinct anatomical structure, and Chinese medicine doesn't actually claim they will be. A meridian is better understood as a map of connection and influence, not a literal pipe carrying a literal substance.

The map itself was not invented from pure imagination. It was built up over centuries from clinical observation: pressing or stimulating a specific point on the body reliably produced an effect somewhere else — sometimes right next to it, sometimes far away, like along the arm or down the leg. Practitioners recorded these connections point by point, and the lines drawn between them, showing which points tended to affect which distant regions together, became the meridians. The map describes a real, observed pattern of influence, even though the "roads" on the map are not literal physical roads.

This distinction matters because it changes what counts as evidence. Looking for a meridian with a scalpel is like looking for a "trade route" with a shovel — you won't find a paved road, because a trade route was never a paved road to begin with. It was a pattern of consistent, repeated connection between two places. Meridians ask to be evaluated the same way: not by dissection, but by whether the pattern of connection they describe holds up, case after case.
paras_zh: 西方讀者第一次聽到經絡——氣被認為在其中運行的通道——時，自然的假設是它們一定是physical的管子，類似血管或神經，只是現代解剖學還沒找到而已。這個假設可以理解，但會走進死胡同。從來沒有任何一條經絡在顯微鏡下被獨立辨識成一個明確的解剖結構，而中醫其實也不主張它們會被找到。經絡更適合被理解成一張連結與影響的地圖，不是一根搬運著一種實質物質的實體管線。
這張地圖本身不是憑空想像出來的。它是好幾個世紀累積下來的臨床觀察建構起來的：按壓或刺激身體上某個特定的點，能穩定地在別的地方——有時候就在旁邊，有時候很遠，像是沿著手臂或腿——產生效果。醫師一個點一個點地記錄這些連結，而點與點之間畫出的連線——顯示哪些點傾向於一起影響哪些遠端區域——就變成了經絡。這張地圖描述的是一個真實、被觀察到的影響模式，即使地圖上的「道路」不是字面意義上的實體道路。
這個分野很重要，因為它改變了什麼才算得上證據。拿手術刀去找一條經絡，就像拿鏟子去找一條「貿易路線」——你不會找到一條鋪好的路，因為貿易路線本來就從來不是一條鋪好的路。它是兩個地方之間一種持續、重複出現的連結模式。經絡也該用同樣的方式來評估：不是靠解剖，而是看它描述的連結模式，是不是一個案例接著一個案例都站得住腳。
